questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The language and the culture. Also the general safety level in the country and distance from home country (= price). The specific place was my second priority so I hadn't looked too much into it beforehand (at all).

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There was no list with all the things we had to do, which I don't understand, as it must be the same for most exchange students, semester after semester. That being said, it was very easy to get in touch with coordinators that could answer my questions (what to do next, which order, where and how do I do that), and they were quick to respond, so there was never any stress or feeling of being lost or abandoned.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a welcome day, and good and quick communication with the relevant office.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: 5 would be that they would have just send out the relevant information, instead of having to ask for it, but once I asked, the response time was quick and accurate and I could always just come to the office (vicedecano de relaciones internacionales) and ask.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, I used milanuncios, saw three flats in one day and went with one them. I paid €225 pr. month which is low-key expensive for Caceres, but then I had two rooms, my own bathroom, and only one roommate. Most people pay around €125 for a room in a flat with 2-3 roommates and shared bathroom.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I didn't hear of anyone who stayed on campus; it's located in the outskirts of the city and only reachable by bus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I just remember doing it step by step, asking at the office of the Vicedecano de relaciones internacionales and following his instructions, then asking him 'and now what?'. He could've spared himself at least five mails and five physical appearances at his office from me, had he send me the info proactively (eg. how to get registered at the Campus Virtual, etc.), but as he was quick to respond so I don't have much to complain about.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Vicedecano de relaciones internacionales was very responsive.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: As I had chosen classes from different years and even different grades (filología hispánica and filología inglesa) there were a lot of classes overlapping. In the end, I had three of the five classes I had chosen beforehand, and had to change the last two.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would say it's pretty chill, it's not like there are any deadlines, the only problem is if you have overlapping classes and have to change some of them, but that's more on the home university to accept your changes. The only thing, really, is if you need access to the campus virtual for some reason before you have it, but then you can ask a classmate to send whatever it is you need, or talk to the teacher.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In two subjects I basically learned nothing (traducción I and II), in two I learned something (lengua española and análisis de discurso) , and in one I learned a lot (variación lingüística). In general, the teachers seemed confused, often they were just rambling on about something irrelevant (a personal anecdote, or just chatting with the students) until the time was up because they didn't have more prepared for that day; there was no homework and only one assignment pr. course (if you choose evaluación continua), and we almost always left half an hour early (because "people had to get home and eat"(??)), or agreed with the teacher to come in half an hour late (because "it was very early" (9 o'clock??). Had I gone for the academic aspect I think I would have been very disappointed.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: There was no public semester plan so you never knew what was gonna happen a given day. There was also no homework although that could have spared tons of time in class. Generally, the teachers didn't upload the slides before the end of the 'tema', so many students would spent the whole class desperately trying to copy down the slides. In some subject the teacher would write something on the blackboard, and then all the students would copy it, and twenty or maybe thirty minutes would pass like that, instead of the teacher just writing it on a computer and uploading to the campus virtual. Soo much of the time spent in the class room could have been given as homework, and then we could've spend the time in class going into depth with it, discussing it, or working actively with it - instead, the classes were mostly about being told something, but there was never time for applying the theory hands on (doing exercises).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
No homework and very little teacher-student interaction. In variación lingüística, for example, the teacher would analyze one or several texts every class, but we never analyzed one ourselves before it came up in the exam. At UCPH, the students would have to do the analysis (often in groups), the teacher would guide the ones who need it, and then in the end you would discuss it between all and the teacher might give her/his take.
During my semester, I can only think of one or two examples of group work.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Lengua española
Traducción I (español-inglés-español)
Traducción II (español-inglés-español)
Análisis del discurso
La variación lingüística en español

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
La variación lingüística was very interesting and the teacher always helpful and friendly.
Lengua española was sometimes interesting, and sometimes it seemed like nonsense. The exams are spread out throughout the semester which is nice.
The translation classes were easy but the teacherm was really unpleasant. I would definitely recommend choosing the global evaluation in the translation classes so you don't have to do a presentation. The exam was super straight forward, just translating two texts, and one theoretical question that weighed very little in the evaluation.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The registration process at the uni costed 5€.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Everything in general; flat, food etc. The monthly bus card was 14,50€/month and then you could use all busses freely.
There's a thing called an 'abono' which you can get with the train (renfe) and bus (alsa), you pay an amount (20-50€) and then you can travel freely between two set destinations (eg. caceres-madrid with train, or caceres-seville with bus).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are a lot of facilities that you can rent (football, paddle, volleyball and tennis pitches etc.), a library, erasmus activities most weeks, and trips.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: football, paddle, volleyball and tennis etc. pitches, a library, a gym that costs €2 euros to use (but it's small and after one time I never came back, one of the two treadmills moved when you used it, for instance). Erasmus activities, parties and trips.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the stuff in the intro week, you'll get to know a lot of people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Barruecos is a nice natural resort with a lot of cows 15 minutes in bus from Caceres where they've shot a GOT dragon-scene.
Lissabon (Sintra) is five hours away, Madrid is three hours away in train, Seville three hours in bus (not a big fan of Seville BUT from there you can go to Málaga, GRANADA(!) and Córdoba - do go watch a flamenco-show!!)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was tough adjusting to the eating schedules, tough with the heat from April and forward, tough that people don't go to the discotecas before 1 or 2 in the morning, but the most difficult thing must be the complete absence of punctuality - when volleyball is scheduled for 5 it maaybe starts at 6:30...

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to the people you sit next to, introduce yourself, I would say the Spanish people I met were easy to talk to and very open, but obviously it might be necessary to take the first step.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The punctuality-thing is difficult to handle for everyone involved.. ("pedimos puntualidad", "vengan yaa", "those of you who have written you name on the event, are you gonna come at all?" etc.)

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: There are tons of small bars everywhere and people sitting out on the streets from winter to summer, it's very nice and lively. The prices of drinks, cinema etc. makes it very easy to meet up with people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Ask the teachers or co-students whenever you're uncertain about something.
Check other subjects before arrival so you're somewhat ready if (when) you have overlapping classes.
I would say I learned a lot from having Spanish (speaking) roommates.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The abonos (renfe and alsa).
The abono mensual (monthly bus card - bring passport photos).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Living in the Spanish culture for several month, experiencing it first hand, talking a lot of Spanish, getting to know people from all over the spanish-speaking world.
Visiting the amazing places you can reach from Cáceres; el Alhambra (buy entrance weeks before), Lissabon, Madrid, Córdoba, Málaga, and with two trains you can reach Barcelona which was a huge experience.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding peace with the structure of the educational system, with so much time wasted every day.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
